solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Covering page in proofreading mark

parts.note: a caret (^) marks where text is to be inserted

explanation.surface: A proofreader's mark scrawled across a page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' reads as the proofreader's mark lying over the page, but it is the definition: a carpet covers a floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: what lies over a floor, the everyday sense of floor covering.

clue.text: Maidservant bearing a ring for religious leader

parts.note: an ayah is a nursemaid or maidservant in India
to ring a bell is to toll it

explanation.surface: A servant carrying a ring on behalf of a cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests O or a piece of jewellery; here it is the verb, to ring a bell, giving TOLL.
explanation.definitionFit: A general description of a specific title: the senior Shiite clerics of Iran hold it.

clue.text: Interest announced for every case

indicators.note: we hear the words spoken rather than see them written

parts.note: per = for every; a suit is a legal case

explanation.surface: A lawyer charging interest on every case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interest' sounds financial beside 'case', but it means a hobby or pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the hobby sense: something you follow in your spare time, as in 'outdoor pursuits'.

clue.text: Time without tea for so many? (A number)

parts.note: w/o is the shorthand for without
surface padding that doubles as a hint, recalling a famous song about tea for a pair

explanation.surface: A time with no tea, wondering how many are coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea for so many?' is a cryptic nod to the song Tea for Two, and the setter adds '(A number)' as the plain definition to make the answer fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the setter's bracketed hint names the class, and the song Tea for Two confirms which member.

clue.text: Silly play's opening provided by cast

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to fling is to cast or throw

explanation.surface: A theatre review: the play's silly first night owed everything to its cast.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre setting makes 'cast' the actors; it is the verb, to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, mostly British: something piffling is trivial and foolish, like piffle, nonsense.

clue.text: Infatuation with a high-ranking Turk

parts.note: a pash is British schoolgirl slang for a crush

explanation.surface: Someone smitten with an Ottoman grandee.
explanation.walkthrough: PASH, an old British slang word for a crush or infatuation, is the piece most solvers outside Britain will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasha was a high-ranking Ottoman Turkish official.

clue.text: Counterfeit sum taking people in is a bloomer

indicators.note: the sum takes the people into itself

parts.note: a tot is a sum, as in tot up

explanation.surface: A forger's fake sum turning out to be a howler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, which suits the forgery; here it is literal, a thing that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The forget-me-not is a small blue flower, so a bloomer.

clue.text: Palace attendant's first opening after noon

indicators.note: take the first letter of attendant

explanation.surface: A palace servant being first to open up after midday.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads backwards from the end: attendant's first letter opens noon to make AN, and 'after' gives LATER in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lateran Palace in Rome was long the papal residence.

clue.text: Nobody is forgetting an old date

indicators.note: is forgets its I, dropping it

parts.note: IS loses I, an = one = I

explanation.surface: Someone who can't remember an old date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An' stands for one, which is I, so IS without I leaves S.
explanation.definitionFit: The nones were a fixed day in each month of the ancient Roman calendar.

clue.text: Mother of pearly king dropped into ocean travelling with us

definitions.note: an adjective hidden in a playful phrase: nacreous means of mother-of-pearl

indicators.note: ocean's letters move about

explanation.surface: The pearly king's mother, with the king thrown overboard on a sea voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mother of pearly' seems to be a mangled phrase; nacre is mother-of-pearl, so NACREOUS means like mother-of-pearl. A pearly king is a Cockney costermonger in a button-covered suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacreous means pearly, having the lustre of mother-of-pearl.

clue.text: Start to tuck into sandwich and roly-poly

indicators.note: the start of tuck is its first letter

parts.note: a round is a sandwich made from two slices of bread

explanation.surface: An instruction to tuck into a sandwich and a jam roly-poly pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Roly-poly is a British pudding, which sits well with tucking in; here it means plump.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: roly-poly describes a round, chubby person, and rotund comes from the Latin for round.

clue.text: Visitor worried after run out in dangerous country

parts.note: r.o. is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out
ate = worried, as in 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: A tourist anxious after being thrown out of a hostile land.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket's run out is written RO on the scorecard; 'after' places the visitor and the worry behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue state is a nation seen as a threat to world peace.

clue.text: Orchestrate unusually sweet composition

indicators.note: the letters are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Scoring a pleasant piece of music in an unusual way.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical words 'orchestrate' and 'composition' point to a pretty tune; the composition is a Viennese chocolate cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Sachertorte is a rich Viennese chocolate cake, a sweet confection.

clue.text: Spots litter leader's left

indicators.note: 'left' as the past of leave: the leader has departed, so the first letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A leopard's spots and her litter's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' and 'litter' suggest an animal family; spots are a skin rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the medical sense: a skin eruption shows as spots.

clue.text: Lake bed holds solidified matter

indicators.note: the bed holds the lake inside it

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A lake bed containing hardened sediment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake bed' reads as one geographical thing; split it into L and COT.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is a lump of thickened, solidified matter such as blood.

clue.text: One miracle involved splendid ritual

indicators.note: the letters are tangled up

explanation.surface: A miracle at the heart of a grand religious rite.
explanation.walkthrough: The miracle points to church, which is fitting: the answer is the grand rite itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceremonial is a formal, stately rite.

clue.text: Have high opinion of endless desert

indicators.note: the last letter is cut off

parts.note: to rate someone is to think highly of them

explanation.surface: Admiring a boundless desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like sand; it is the verb, to abandon, as in to rat on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to desert, as a rat leaves a sinking ship.

clue.text: Current work eliminating area's gradual growth

indicators.note: the A is removed from creation

explanation.surface: Electrical work that stops a region from slowly expanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present-day', but it is electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym from geology and biology: layers building up bit by bit.

clue.text: Writer of short musical and rotten novel

indicators.note: rotten's letters are made new
the musical is cut short by a letter

parts.note: Chess, the Tim Rice musical, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A playwright who wrote a brief show and a dreadful book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' seems to be the writer's book, but it is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: G.K. Chesterton was an English writer, creator of Father Brown.

clue.text: Made a great effort as stone cracked

definitions.note: 'Made a great effort' stands as a past participle, as in 'have made a great effort'

parts.note: st = stone, the British unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone working hard at breaking stone.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight (14 pounds), abbreviated ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Striven is the past participle of strive: having made a great effort.

clue.text: Be confronted by heartless travesty

indicators.note: the middle letter is removed

parts.note: a farce is a travesty; lose its middle R

explanation.surface: Having to confront a cruel mockery of justice.
explanation.walkthrough: FARCE has five letters, so its heart is the R.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the passive sense, as in 'we face a problem'.

clue.text: Run out of fortress, free in wild areas

indicators.note: the remaining letters are set loose

parts.note: r = run, the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A prisoner escaping from a castle, free in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' reads as the escapee's liberty; it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose description: large tracts of woodland are among the wildest land left.

clue.text: Almost terrifying disfigurement

indicators.note: the last letter is left off

explanation.surface: A nearly horrifying blemish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims just the final letter, so SCARY loses its Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a mark left on the skin by a healed wound.

clue.text: Check address of page, an old peasant

parts.note: a URL is the address of a web page

explanation.surface: Checking where a page boy of old lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Page' suggests a medieval servant, suiting the peasant; here it is a web page.
explanation.definitionFit: A churl was a medieval peasant of the lowest rank.

clue.text: Discuss business while gobbling?

parts.note: the plain sense: get down to frank negotiation
the surface pushes greedy eating; the setter means the noise a certain farmyard bird makes

explanation.surface: Doing a business deal over a big meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gobbling' suggests eating greedily; a turkey gobbles, so gobbling is talking turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the American phrase means to speak frankly about business, and the question mark flags the literal turkey talk.

clue.text: Spring's past, meadow pipit's content to fly away

indicators.note: the inside of pipit leaves

parts.note: pipit without its inner letters IPI

explanation.surface: Spring is over, and the meadow pipit is happy to migrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring's past' sounds like the season ending; it means the past tense of the verb spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapt is the past tense of leap, meaning spring.

clue.text: Tremble when delivering note

definitions.meaning: a voice shaking as it speaks, the verb sense
a musical note, the British name for an eighth note

explanation.surface: A nervous speaker's voice shaking over a message.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a voice trembling as it speaks; the second is the musical note, an eighth note.
explanation.definitionFit: To quaver is to tremble in speaking; a quaver is also a musical note.

clue.text: A couple of short marks, wrong and right: initially this makes sense

indicators.note: each mark loses its last letter

parts.note: a cross marks an answer wrong; short, so CROSS loses an S
a tick marks an answer right; short, so TICK loses its K
announces the two marks that follow, each cut short

explanation.surface: A teacher's marking: a cross and a tick, and the first letters spell out the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A couple of short marks' tells you there are two marks, both cut short, named by what they mean: wrong and right.
explanation.definitionFit: In an acrostic the initial letters of lines spell out a word or message.

clue.text: This legendary bird rises into heavens!

indicators.note: in a down clue, the answer read upwards becomes the other word

parts.note: cor! is a British exclamation, like heavens!

explanation.surface: A mythical bird soaring up to the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavens' looks like the sky the bird flies into; with its exclamation mark it is the cry COR!, which is ROC read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The roc is a giant legendary bird of Arabian tales.

clue.text: Most inscrutable spy's heading under cover?

indicators.note: a word's heading is its first letter

explanation.surface: An unreadable spy heading off undercover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under cover' reads as the spy working in secret; literally the S goes under the blanket.
explanation.definitionFit: Blankest means most expressionless, hence most inscrutable.

clue.text: Function in business without Latin

parts.note: sine is the Latin for without

explanation.surface: An event held at a firm with no Latin spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without Latin' seems to mean lacking Latin; it asks for the Latin word for without.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: cosine is one of the trigonometric functions, alongside sine and tangent.
